title: Sable and the Postcard
premise: August Ravensworth walked off the stage mid-concerto eleven years ago and never touched a cello in public again, burying her career, her mother's death, and an unsent letter to the woman she loved. When a postcard arrives postmarked from that same year—written by her first love, Ilsa, and lost in the mail—it reveals Ilsa never stopped waiting. August returns to the coastal town where it all ended, only to find Ilsa is now engaged and running her late father's music shop, while August's estranged brother contests their mother's house, the one place August's past still lives. As August repairs the shop's broken instruments and slowly repairs herself, she must choose between the safe invisibility she's built and risking everything for a love that refuses to stay in the past tense. In the end, August performs again—at Ilsa's wedding rehearsal dinner, which becomes something else entirely—and claims both the house and the heart she once abandoned.
about_author: Lena Crane is a former orchestral librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's love letters tucked inside borrowed sheet music before writing her own stories. She lives on the Oregon coast with her partner and a badly tuned upright piano.

chapters.title: The Unplayed Room
chapters.summary: August's POV. Ten years after walking off stage mid-performance, August teaches cello to children who will never know she was nearly great. A postcard arrives, postmarked eleven years ago, in handwriting she'd know anywhere: 'Come home when you're ready. I'll wait.' She doesn't open the door of her mother's old practice room that night. Emotional beat: dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Return Postage
chapters.summary: August's POV. Her brother Marcus calls: he's selling their mother's house unless August comes back to sign. She drives to Greywater Bay, telling herself it's about the house, not the postcard's sender. The town has changed; the music shop hasn't. Through the window she sees Ilsa Merrow, older, laughing with someone wearing an engagement ring. Emotional beat: the past arriving faster than courage.

chapters.title: What the Mail Lost
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Ilsa recognizes August instantly at the hardware store and says nothing about the postcard—the one she wrote the night August left, returned to her last month by a retiring postal worker. Engaged to practical, kind Dr. Nadia Okafor, Ilsa tells herself the letter belongs in a drawer. But she can't stop watching August carry boxes into the Ravensworth house. Emotional beat: guilt sharpened by hope.

chapters.title: Broken Instruments
chapters.summary: August's POV. To delay signing the house papers, August offers to restore the damaged inventory in Ilsa's shop—a skill learned from her mother. Working side by side, they orbit old wounds without naming them. Ilsa mentions the engagement casually; August congratulates her with steady hands and a splitting chest. Emotional beat: intimacy rebuilt on avoidance.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Winter
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Nadia notices Ilsa humming the concerto August abandoned—the piece Ilsa played the night they met. Flashback threads reveal the truth: August fled after her mother's death and a devastating review, believing Ilsa would be better off unburdened. Ilsa never got to argue. Now the argument is eleven years late and she's promised herself to someone else. Emotional beat: grief for a choice made for you.

chapters.title: The House That Remembers
chapters.summary: August's POV. Marcus arrives to force the sale and finds August sleeping in her childhood room, surrounded by her mother's sheet music. Their fight cracks open the family secret: their mother's final years were paid for by August's abandoned career—every lesson fee, every hospital bill. Survival had a price, and August paid it alone. Marcus leaves shaken; August finally opens the locked practice room. Emotional beat: inheritance as wound.

chapters.title: Tuning Fork
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Ilsa finds August asleep in the shop among repaired instruments, and the drawer with the unsent postcard stands open between them. The confrontation is quiet and devastating: 'You decided for me.' August admits she chose disappearance over being seen failing. They part unresolved—Ilsa to Nadia, August to the empty house—but neither can play anything afterward except that concerto. Emotional beat: truth spoken too late to be simple.

chapters.title: Intermission
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Both women try to return to their lives. Nadia, perceptive and decent, asks Ilsa one question: 'Do you love me, or do you love not being alone?' Meanwhile Marcus returns—not to fight, but to withdraw the sale, having found their mother's will leaving the house to whoever 'comes back to play.' August realizes staying invisible was never survival; it was just slower loss. Emotional beat: the cost of safety itemized.

chapters.title: The Concerto
chapters.summary: August's POV. At Ilsa and Nadia's rehearsal dinner, the town asks August to play something for the couple. She sits down at the cello for the first time in eleven years, hands shaking, and plays the concerto through to its end—the ending she never gave anyone. Halfway through, she looks up and finds Ilsa crying in the front row. The performance becomes a confession witnessed by everyone. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into offering.

chapters.title: Come Home When You're Ready
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Ilsa ends the engagement honestly, giving Nadia the grace she was denied at twenty-four. Weeks later, August nails a new sign over the shop door: MERROW & RAVENSWORTH, REPAIRS AND LESSONS. In the restored practice room of the house she kept, August writes a reply to the eleven-year-old postcard and mails it to the address across town. It arrives the next morning. Emotional beat: love in the present tense, at last.
